analysis.one_liner: Bans foreign-controlled and foreign-owned companies from spending money in U.S. elections.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by Rep. Jamie Raskin with 35 Democratic cosponsors, the bill never left the House Administration Committee and died without a vote when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would extend the existing ban on foreign nationals' election money to American-registered companies that are controlled, influenced, or owned by foreign nationals — for example, any company where a foreign owner holds 1% or more, where foreign owners together hold 5%, or where a foreign national can direct the company's U.S. election spending. Any company funding elections would have to file a sworn certification that it is not foreign-controlled, and groups receiving its money could only use it if they got that certification and kept the funds segregated. It would also make clear that the foreign money ban covers state and local ballot measures and money flowing to super PACs, and would require corporate political action committees to certify each year that no foreign national influences their spending decisions.
analysis.who_benefits: American voters, who would get a firmer shield against foreign governments and foreign owners financing U.S. campaigns and ballot fights through domestic companies. American candidates and parties also benefit because they could not accept corporate money without proof that it is not foreign-controlled.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the current ban on foreign nationals' campaign contributions and expenditures to domestic business entities that are foreign-controlled, foreign-influenced, or foreign-owned — including companies where a foreign national holds 50% or more of ownership, just 1% of ownership, or 5% in aggregate among foreign owners, or where a foreign national can direct the company's U.S. election spending.

Requires a company's chief executive to certify to the Federal Election Commission, under penalty of perjury, within 7 days of any election-related spending that the entity is not a foreign national, and bars campaign committees and others from using corporate money unless they receive that certification and account for the funds separately.

Closes specific channels: it states that the foreign money ban covers spending on state and local ballot initiatives and disbursements to super PACs, and it requires corporate PACs to certify annually that U.S. citizens or permanent residents manage them, that no foreign national participates in their decisions, and that foreign board members abstain from votes about the fund.

analysis.who_pays: Foreign-owned and foreign-controlled companies and their U.S. operations, which would lose the ability to fund American elections and would face new certification, ownership-disclosure, and segregated-accounting costs. Domestic companies with any foreign ownership would also bear compliance costs, and corporate PACs would take on annual certification requirements.

drawbacks.text: The trigger is very low: a corporation in which a single foreign shareholder holds just 1% — or several foreign holders together 5% — would be barred entirely from election spending, sweeping in some U.S. companies with widely held foreign institutional ownership and raising questions about overbreadth.

Enforcement leans on self-certification: the system depends on chief executives truthfully swearing they made 'due inquiry' and on recipients segregating and accounting for certified funds, so its strength depends on how rigorously violations are investigated and punished.

The bill would take effect 180 days after enactment regardless of whether the Federal Election Commission has written any regulations to implement it, which could leave companies and campaign committees to comply without official guidance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real gap: foreign nationals are already barred from funding U.S. elections, but money can move through American-registered companies with foreign ownership or influence. The compliance costs fall mainly on the entities being regulated, not on ordinary people. The honest trade-off is overbreadth — the 1% ownership threshold and the self-certification paperwork would burden some genuinely domestic companies — but those costs are administrative, while the stakes for election integrity are structural. A modest, targeted bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Jamie Raskin introduced the bill on December 14, 2021, with 19 original cosponsors; it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the same day.
The bill grew to 35 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and none of its provisions ever received a committee markup, a floor vote, or action in the Senate.
The complete action history shows no activity after the initial referral; the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign-owned and foreign-influenced companies and big-money groups are better off because the bill died — they keep spending in U.S. elections without any new certification or disclosure requirements. Incumbent campaigns that prefer not to vet corporate donations also avoided the change.

for.name: Jamie Raskin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 19 original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 14, 2021 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress — no markup, no vote.

against.name: Zoe Lofgren
against.role: Chair, House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote; it sat untouched until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 35 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and because the bill never reached a vote, no member ever had to record a position.

industries.note: They would lose the ability to fund U.S. federal, state, and local elections through American-registered entities, and their executives would face sworn certification and ownership-disclosure duties. What they would give up is influence over American elections that current law leaves reachable through domestic subsidiaries.

industries.industry: Super PACs and outside spending groups
industries.note: The bill would bar them from taking disbursements from companies lacking a foreign-money certification and from any committee that accepts funds not compliant with campaign finance law, cutting off a channel for foreign-influenced corporate money.

Corporate PACs would have to certify annually that U.S. citizens or permanent residents manage them, that no foreign national shapes their spending decisions, and that foreign directors abstain from fund votes — new compliance conditions on money they currently raise and spend without such vetting.
